nameStory: Marsh cinquefoil gets its name from the French word 'cinq' meaning five, referring to its five leaflets that spread out like fingers on a hand. The 'marsh' part is obvious once you see where it grows - always near water in boggy, swampy places where your boots might get wet!
description: Marsh cinquefoil is a low-growing, spreading shrub that loves to get its feet wet in marshes and along pond edges. This member of the rose family grows about 1-2 feet tall and spreads by underground stems called rhizomes, often forming patches. Unlike most roses, it produces distinctive dark red to purple flowers instead of the typical pink or white blooms, and its compound leaves have five serrated leaflets.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dark red to purple flowers with five petals that feel papery when touched - very unusual for the rose family and quite striking against the green foliage

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves divided into five sharp-toothed leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand, with a slightly fuzzy texture underneath

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading subshrub that often has stems and leaves floating on water or sprawling across wet mud - you'll often see it partly submerged

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dry fruits clustered together on a spongy, enlarged receptacle that turns reddish-brown and feels somewhat cork-like

habitat: Look for marsh cinquefoil in wet, boggy areas throughout New England - pond edges, marshy spots along streams, and wetland margins where the soil stays consistently moist. It thrives in acidic, peaty soils and is often found growing with sedges, cattails, and other water-loving plants. You'll typically find it in cooler, northern parts of the region where it can spread into shallow water.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges from rhizomes, and the distinctive five-fingered leaves begin to unfurl along wet margins.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season when the unusual dark red-purple flowers appear, making identification easiest during this time.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and fruits ripen to reddish-brown, while leaves may take on reddish tints before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to underground rhizomes, leaving little trace above ground in frozen wetlands.

funFact: Scientists have successfully crossed marsh cinquefoil with strawberry plants to create ornamental hybrids, combining the water-loving abilities of cinquefoil with strawberry genetics - imagine a strawberry that could grow in a swamp!
confusionNotes: The dark red-purple flowers are so unusual that marsh cinquefoil is rarely confused with other plants when in bloom. Out of flower, the five-leaflet pattern might be mistaken for wild strawberry, but strawberry has white flowers and grows in dry areas, while marsh cinquefoil sticks to wet spots.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'cinquefoil,' this plant was recently moved from the Potentilla genus (where most cinquefoils live) into its own genus Comarum, reflecting its unique adaptations to aquatic life. You might still see it listed as Potentilla palustris in older field guides.
compareHints: Marsh cinquefoil is the only species in the Comarum genus in New England, making it unique among local rose family members. Unlike other cinquefoils in the Potentilla genus which have yellow flowers and grow in dry areas, marsh cinquefoil stands out with its purple flowers and wetland habitat. It's the only rose family member in our region that's truly aquatic in its lifestyle.
